articleTitle: A view of lean manufacture from an automotive electronics designer
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Smart Design for Lean Manufacture
abstract: The primary goal of the design process is to remain in business. The case study presented here by the authors is that of an electronics department which, from external appearances, 'just grew' from a few to about 160 people over a period of ten years, during which time the company has gone from public to foreign ownership. The number of electronics designers has been static for about four years.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Smart Design for Lean Manufacture
abstract: The electronic design problem has reached new complexities with VLSI with problems of access to test and very high production engineering costs. In this context, lean manufacture is getting the design right so there is no rework and the design is centred on the process norms so that there are no marginal design states to affect reliability. The background to this presentation is the simulation of computer hardware design, one of the smartest design methods within the author's experience. The problems of simulation are that it is costly, both in time and resource and there is no prescribed "end point". Lean design is when just enough simulation has been completed to ensure "right first time design" of the VLSI and the printed circuit boards that make up a computer and a design can be confidently committed to manufacture.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Smart Design for Lean Manufacture
abstract: A great deal of effort has been devoted to the adoption of "Japanese" manufacturing methods: cells; JIT; Kanban and the rest. The majority of British manufacturing companies have adopted these techniques to some extent; many have virtually no activities planned and managed on any other basis. This paper is about creating value and reducing cost by simplification, focused performance improvement and targeting progressive product development over a period of years.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A case study from Cincinnati Milacron (lean manufacture smart design)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Smart Design for Lean Manufacture
abstract: During the later half of the 1980s the management team running the UK operations of Cincinnati Milacron based in Birmingham realised that there were significant problems facing the company if it were to survive into the next century as a leading manufacturer of CNC machine tools. The management team realised what was necessary-a complete re-design of both the companies' product range and the methods used to introduce, develop, and produce equipment in high volumes at low cost. The methodology which it was decided to adopt was based on that used successfully by the Japanese motor manufacturers, which had enabled them to dramatically reduce design, development and pre-production phases of new car introduction. This coupled with high quality and aggressive pricing had, as with the Japanese machine tool industry, led to massive penetration of world export markets.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Re-engineering of company processes and the benefits
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Smart Design for Lean Manufacture
abstract: The author argues that a contributing element to the UK manufacturing base recovery can be provided if a smart design capability is adopted, integrated with lean manufacturing. Previous papers have adequately narrated the need for streamlining of the product evolutionary process from concept to product delivery. They have also provided some interesting and encouraging statistics on the benefits they have achieved. These are not isolated instances but are representative of improvement in performance experienced by a growing number of companies now better able to compete successfully in the market place.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
